title: Perpetuity: cash flows forever
subtitle: A level cash flow that continues indefinitely
openingQuestion: PV Perpetuity = PMT / r. If you receive 10 million/year forever at r = 10%, what is it worth today?
explanation: A perpetuity is a level cash flow that continues forever, and the counterintuitive part is that its total present value is still finite: cash flows far in the future get discounted down toward zero, so the series converges. The formula reduces to the cash flow divided by the discount rate, or divided by the difference between the discount rate and the growth rate if the cash flow grows steadily. This is exactly the formula used to calculate terminal value in every discounted cash flow model.

diagram.label: A level cash flow continuing indefinitely
Distant cash flows get discounted down toward zero
So the total is still finite: PV = C / r
With steady growth, the denominator becomes (r − g)

realWorldExample.company: Preferred stock paying a fixed dividend forever
realWorldExample.description: Some preferred stock commits to paying a fixed dividend forever, with no maturity date - this is the closest real-world example to the theoretical concept of a perpetuity, and it is priced exactly with the PV Perpetuity formula.

quiz.question: What is the PV formula for a growing perpetuity?
options: C × (r − g), multiplying instead of dividing by the spread
C / r, i.e. the formula for a non-growing perpetuity
C × r, multiplying the cash flow by the required cost of capital
C / (r − g), where g is the perpetual growth rate
quiz.explanation: PV = C / (r − g). Used in the Gordon Growth Model to compute Terminal Value in a DCF. It's highly sensitive to g: if g is close to r, PV blows up toward infinity - a common source of 'garbage in' results in DCF models.

quiz.question: Why does a cash flow that lasts FOREVER (a perpetuity) have a FINITE present value, instead of tending toward infinity?
options: Because the further out a cash flow is, the more heavily it's discounted, so the sum still converges
Because in practice no one lives long enough to receive an infinite cash flow
Because the formula is technically wrong but still accepted in practice
A perpetuity actually has no well-defined present value at all
quiz.explanation: This is a neat mathematical result: even though you're adding infinitely many terms, if each term shrinks geometrically (because of discounting), the sum still converges to a finite value = C/r.

quiz.question: A fixed dividend of 10 million VND/year forever, discount rate 8%. What is the PV?
options: 80 million (= 10 × 8, multiplying instead of dividing by r)
125 million (= 10 ÷ 0.08, cash flow divided by the rate)
12.5 million (= 10 ÷ 0.8, off by a decimal place)
Infinite, because the cash flow never ends
quiz.explanation: PV = C / r = 10/0.08 = 125 million. An infinite cash flow still gives a finite value, because each year further out is divided by an ever-larger denominator, and that series converges.

quiz.question: Gordon Growth: C = 100 billion, r = 10%, g = 4%. What is the Terminal Value?
options: 2,500 billion (= 100 ÷ 0.04, mistakenly dividing by g)
1,000 billion (= 100 ÷ 0.10, ignoring the growth rate g)
1,667 billion (= 100 ÷ (0.10 − 0.04), dividing by r minus g)
714 billion (= 100 ÷ (0.10 + 0.04), adding instead of subtracting)
quiz.explanation: PV = C / (r − g) = 100/0.06 ≈ 1,667 billion. The denominator is only 6%, so it's extremely sensitive: raising g from 4% to 5% pushes the result to 2,000 billion, a 20% jump from a single assumption.

quiz.question: Why must the assumed g in a Gordon Growth model be lower than the long-run growth rate of the economy?
options: Because real cash flows never actually grow that fast
Because the formula returns a negative result once g exceeds 5% a year
Because valuation standards cap g at the target inflation rate
Because otherwise the company would end up larger than the entire economy
quiz.explanation: g applies for an infinite number of years. A company growing 8% forever inside an economy growing 3% would gradually consume the entire economy - which is impossible. This is why g is usually capped somewhere near long-run GDP growth.

keyTakeaways: Used for Terminal Value in DCF - highly sensitive to the g assumption

practicePrompt.question: A preferred stock pays a fixed dividend of 8 million VND/year forever (with no end date). If the appropriate discount rate is 10%/year, what is the present value (PV) of this entire perpetual dividend stream?
options: PV of a Perpetuity = C / r = 8 / 0.1 = 80 million dong, discounting the stream at 10% forever
PV = C × r = 8 × 0.1 = 0.8 million VND, multiplying the dividend directly by the discount rate
PV cannot be calculated for a cash flow that lasts forever because there's no end date to compute against
PV = C × n where n is the number of years, but since n is infinite, PV must also be infinite
practicePrompt.explanation: PV Perpetuity = C / r = 8/0.1 = 80 million VND. This simple formula applies to a level cash flow that continues forever (a perpetuity) - even though the cash flow is infinite in time, its present value is still finite because each future payment gets discounted down to an ever-smaller amount.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Calculate a PV Perpetuity
application.message: Suppose you have a level income stream that lasts forever (for example, a dividend), try calculating PV = C/r at a few different discount rates to see how the value changes.
application.secondary: This is exactly how Terminal Value is calculated in a DCF model.

sections.text: A perpetuity is a special kind of annuity: a level cash flow that continues forever, with no end date. It sounds absurd to value something infinite, but thanks to discounting, the present value of a perpetuity is a finite number, and a very simple one to calculate.

PV = C / r, where C is the cash flow per period and r is the discount rate. **Example:** a preferred stock commits to a fixed dividend of 10 million VND/year forever, at a discount rate of 10%: PV = 10 / 0.1 = 100 million VND. Even though the cash flow runs forever, the total present value is just 100 million VND - because dividends far in the future carry almost no value after being discounted so many times.

When the cash flow isn't fixed but grows steadily at a rate g each year, the formula becomes PV = C / (r − g) - this is exactly the Gordon Growth Model, the standard tool for calculating Terminal Value in a DCF model. **Example:** next year's projected cash flow is 50 billion VND, growing at g = 3%/year, r = 10%: PV = 50 / (0.1 − 0.03) = 50 / 0.07 ≈ 714 billion VND.

items: PV Perpetuity converges to a finite value because each term shrinks geometrically as it gets discounted
A growing perpetuity is extremely sensitive as g approaches r - the shrinking denominator (r−g) causes PV to spike unreasonably
The g used in the Gordon Growth Model should not exceed the long-run GDP growth rate
Terminal Value often accounts for 60-80% of total DCF value - which is why the g assumption matters more than almost any other assumption in the model

lines: Perpetuity is a beautiful example of how financial math isn't always intuitive - infinity added up can still come out to a finite number.
